text: Scene 9
speaker: C2

text: C2 turns the frame round to reveal a picture of Dorian’s library
speaker: C2

text: The Picture
speaker: C4/2

text: It was dawn before he reached his home after aimlessly wandering through London.  As he entered his room, his portrait gazed out of the shadows.
speaker: C1

text: The face appeared to him to be a little changed. The expression looked different.
speaker: C2/P

text: One would have said that there was a touch of cruelty in the mouth.
speaker: C3

text: He pulled the window blinds and bright dawn flooded the room and swept away the fantastic shadows into dusky corners, where they lay shuddering.
speaker: C4

text: But the strange expression that he had noticed in the face of the portrait seemed to linger there
speaker: C2/P

text: The sunlight showed him the lines of cruelty round the mouth as clearly as if he had been looking into a mirror after he had done some dreadful thing.
speaker: C3

text: He winced and, taking up from the table an oval glass glanced hurriedly into its polished depths. No line like that warped his red lips.
speaker: C4

text: Suddenly there flashed across his mind what he had said in Basil Hallward's studio. He had uttered a mad wish that he himself might remain young, and the portrait grow old.
speaker: C5

text: How sad it is! I shall grow old, and horrible, and dreadful.  But this picture will remain always young.  If it were only the other way!  If it were I who was to be always young, and the picture that was to grow old! For that - for that - I would give everything! I would give my soul for that!
speaker: C2/P

text: That his own beauty might be untarnished, and the face on the canvas bear the burden of his passions and his sins.
speaker: C1

text: Surely his wish had not been fulfilled?  Such things were impossible.  And, yet, there was the picture before him, with the touch of cruelty in the mouth.
speaker: C6/D

text: Cruelty!  Had he been cruel?  It was the girl's fault, not his.  He had given his love to her. Then she had disappointed him.
speaker: C5

text: And, yet, a feeling of infinite regret came over him, as he thought of her lying at his feet sobbing.
speaker: C3

text: He remembered with what callousness he had watched her.
speaker: C4

text: But he had suffered also.  During the three terrible hours that the play had lasted, he had lived centuries of pain, aeon upon aeon of torture.  His life was well worth hers.
speaker: C6/D

text: Besides, women were better suited to bear sorrow than men.  They only thought of their emotions.  Lord Henry had told him that, and Lord Henry knew what women were.  Why should he trouble about Sibyl Vane?  She was nothing to him now.
speaker: C5

text: But the picture?  What was he to say of that?  It held the secret of his life, and told his story.  It had taught him to love his own beauty.  Would it teach him to loathe his own soul?
speaker: C3

text: For every sin that he committed, a stain would fleck and wreck its fairness.  But he would not sin. He would not listen to Lord Henry’s poisonous theories anymore.
speaker: C1

text: He would go back to Sybil Vane and make amends, marry her, try to love her again. He sat and wrote a passionate letter, imploring her forgiveness.
speaker: C3

text: He fell asleep feeling he had been absolved,
speaker: C1

text: (There is loud knocking - he jerks awake)
speaker: Stage

text: My dear boy, I must see you.
speaker: Lord H

text: (Dorian draws the screen in front of his portrait)
speaker: Stage

text: (enters) I am so sorry for it all, Dorian. But you must not think too much about it.
speaker: Lord H

text: Do you mean about Sibyl Vane?
speaker: Dorian

text: Yes, of course. It is dreadful but it was not your fault.  Tell me, did you go behind and see her, after the play was over?
speaker: Lord H

text: Yes I was brutal, Harry - perfectly brutal.  But it is all right now.  I am not sorry for anything that has happened.  It has taught me to know myself better
speaker: Dorian

text: Ah, Dorian, I am so glad you take it in that way!  I was afraid I would find you plunged in remorse.
speaker: Lord H

text: I have got through all that. I am perfectly happy now.  I know what conscience is. It is not what you told me it was.  It is the divinest thing in us.  Don't sneer at it, Harry. I want to be good.  I can't bear the idea of my soul being hideous.
speaker: Dorian

text: A very charming artistic basis for ethics, Dorian!  I congratulate you on it. But how are you going to begin?
speaker: Lord H

text: By marrying Sibyl Vane.
speaker: Dorian

text: Marrying Sibyl Vane! But, my dear Dorian..
speaker: Lord H

text: Yes, Harry, I know what you are going to say. Something dreadful about marriage.  Don't say it.  Don't ever say things of that kind to me again. She is to be my wife.
speaker: Dorian

text: You know nothing then?
speaker: Lord H

text: What do you mean?
speaker: Dorian

text: (taking both his hands) Dorian don't be frightened. I have to tell you that Sibyl Vane is dead.
speaker: Lord H

text: Dead!  It is not true!  It is a horrible lie!  How dare you say it?
speaker: Dorian

text: It is in all the morning papers. There will have to be an inquest, of course, and you must not be mixed up in it. I suppose they don't know your name at the theatre?  If they don't, it is all right.
speaker: Lord H

text: An Inquest?  Did Sibyl..
speaker: Dorian

text: I have no doubt it was not an accident, Dorian, though it must be put in that way to the public.  It seems that as she was leaving the theatre with her mother, or so, she said she had forgotten something upstairs.  They waited some time for her, but she did not come down again.  They ultimately found her lying dead on the floor of her dressing-room. She had swallowed something ..it had either prussic acid or white lead in it. She seems to have died instantaneously.
speaker: Lord H

text: Sibyl acts going up to her room and taking poison during speech
speaker: Stage

text: Harry it is terrible!
speaker: Dorian

text: Yes; it is very tragic, of course, but you must not get yourself mixed up in it.  Dorian, you mustn't let this thing get on your nerves.
speaker: Lord H

text: So I have murdered Sibyl Vane. Murdered her as surely as if I had cut her little throat with a knife. If I had read all this in a book, Harry, I think I would have wept over it. Somehow, now that it has happened and to me, it seems far too unbelievable for tears. Here is the first passionate love-letter I have ever written in my life.  And it is addressed to a dead girl.  I loved her once!  Then last night she played so badly, and my heart almost broke. She explained it all to me. But I was not moved a bit.  I thought her shallow.  Later something happened that made me afraid. I felt I had done wrong.  And now she is dead. Harry, what shall I do?  You don't know the danger I am in. She would've kept me straight. She had no right to kill herself.  It was selfish of her.
speaker: Dorian

text: My dear Dorian.  If you had married this girl, you would have been wretched… the whole thing would have been an absolute failure.
speaker: Lord H

text: I suppose it would.  But I thought it was my duty.  It is not my fault that this terrible tragedy has prevented my doing what was right. Harry why is it that I cannot feel this tragedy as much as I want to? It seems to me to be simply like a wonderful ending to a Greek tragedy, a tragedy in which I took a great part, but by which I have not been wounded.
speaker: Dorian

text: Chorus and Sibyl get ready to enact the end of a Greek Tragedy
speaker: Stage

text: I wish that I had had such an experience. You are more fortunate than I am. I assure you, Dorian, that not one of the women I have known would have done for me what Sibyl Vane did for you. There is something to me quite beautiful about her death. You must think of that lonely death in the tawdry dressing-room simply as a fragment from some Greek tragedy.  The girl never really lived, and so she has never really died.
speaker: Lord H

text: I have felt all that, but somehow I was afraid of it. I will no longer think of what Sibyl put me through that night at the theatre.  She has atoned for everything by the sacrifice she has made of her life.
speaker: Dorian

text: Chorus enact beautiful suicide Greek style!
speaker: Stage

text: It has been a marvellous experience. That is all.  I wonder if life has still in store for me anything as marvellous.
speaker: Dorian

text: I will send you a book Dorian that will answer that question. You will find all that life holds if you follow its guidance. You will join me at the opera tonight?
speaker: Lord H

text: I think I will Harry. Isn’t Patti singing. I believe it will suit my melancholic mood.
speaker: Dorian

text: (after Lord H leaves Dorian rushes to the portrait)
speaker: Stage

text: You had the news of Sibyl Vane’s death before I did.
speaker: Dorian

text: The time had come to make his choice.
speaker: C1

text: Or had his choice already been made?
speaker: C2

text: Life had decided for him. Eternal youth, infinite passion, pleasures subtle and secret, wild joys and wilder sins - he was to have all these things.
speaker: C3

text: The portrait was to bear the burden of his shame.
speaker: C4

text: He hesitated.
speaker: C5

text: Was it to become a monstrous and loathsome thing,
speaker: C1

text: To be hidden away in a locked room,
speaker: C3

text: to be shut out from the sunlight.
speaker: C4

text: The pity of it!
speaker: All

text: And yet, who would surrender the chance of remaining always young,
speaker: C5

text: however fantastic that chance might be,
speaker: C1

text: or with what fateful consequences it might be fraught?
speaker: C2

text: If the picture was to alter,
speaker: C6/D

text: it was to alter.
speaker: C1

text: Why inquire too closely?
speaker: All

text: He would be able to follow his mind into its secret places.
speaker: C6/D

text: This portrait would be to him the most magical of mirrors.
speaker: C5

text: It would reveal to him his own soul.
speaker: All

text: Not one blossom of his loveliness would ever fade.
speaker: C2

text: Not one pulse of his life would ever weaken.
speaker: C3

text: He would be safe.  That was everything.
speaker: All

text: But the portrait must be hidden away from the eyes of others.
speaker: C6/D

text: He rang the bell for his housekeeper.
speaker: C4

text: After a few moments, Mrs. Leaf bustled into the library.
speaker: Mrs L

text: He asked her for the key of the schoolroom.
speaker: C5

text: The old schoolroom, Mr. Dorian? Why, it is full of dust.  I must put it straight before you go into it. It is not fit for you to see, sir.
speaker: Mrs L

text: I don't want it put straight, Leaf.  I only want the key.
speaker: Dorian

text: Well, sir, you'll be covered with cobwebs if you go into it.  Why, it hasn't been opened for nearly five years - not since his lordship died.
speaker: Mrs L

text: That does not matter.  Give me the key.
speaker: Dorian

text: And here is the key, sir I’ll have it off the bunch in a moment.  But you don't think of living up there, sir, and you so comfortable here?
speaker: Mrs L

text: No, no. Thank you, Leaf.  That will do.
speaker: Dorian

text: Oh Sir, I quite forgot.  Lord Wotton left something for you. (She produces a book from her apron pocket Dorian opens it and sits)
speaker: Mrs Leaf
